The international prospective observational DOAC-CVT study enrolled 619 patients with CVT between 2021 and 2024, demonstrating that during a 6-month follow-up, rates of recurrent thrombosis and major bleeding did not differ between patients treated with DOAC vs vitamin K antagonists. The 12-month results of the EXCOA-CVT cluster RCT and prospective cohort study showed no significant difference in recurrent venous thromboembolism or major bleeding risk between short-term (3–6 months) and long-term (12 months) anticoagulation, in patients with CVT without indication for permanent anticoagulation (conference presentation; preliminary). The 24-month follow-up is ongoing. For cervical artery dissection, the retrospective STOP-CAD study (over 4000 patients) showed no overall association between anticoagulation and ischaemic stroke recurrence at 6 months compared with antiplatelet therapy. However, a secondary analysis demonstrated that patients with occlusive dissection who received anticoagulation experienced lower recurrence risk compared to antiplatelet therapy. An individual patient data meta-analysis of CADISS and TREAT-CAD trials ( n = 444) showed fewer primary endpoint events with anticoagulation vs antiplatelets (1.4% vs 4.4%), although the difference was not statistically significant. Additionally, during the extended follow-up period of TREAT-CAD, outcomes between 3 and 6 months after randomisation were rare, occurred at similar rates in both groups and were exclusively haemorrhagic events. In a registry study of females with prior cervical artery dissection, pregnancy was not associated with an increased overall long-term risk, though event rates were numerically higher during pregnancy through postpartum (3.17%/year) vs outside pregnancy (0.67%/year), with all recurrent dissections occurring in the 6-week postpartum period. Potential practice implications Interventions addressing both traditional risk factors (obesity, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia) and non-traditional factors (migraine management, stress reduction) may be relevant for comprehensive prevention strategies in young-onset stroke. In CVT patients, direct oral anticoagulants may be considered a reasonable treatment option compared with vitamin K antagonists. More data are awaited on optimal treatment duration of anticoagulation in patients without indication for permanent treatment. In cervical artery dissection, both anticoagulants and antiplatelets can be considered; when balancing benefits and risks, it is reasonable to consider occlusive dissection status in individualised decision-making regarding a short course of anticoagulation. In women with prior cervical artery dissection, pregnancy does not increase overall long-term risk, though the risk may be elevated in the postpartum period. Key limitations and gaps The main limitation in young-stroke studies is observational study design, leading to lower-quality evidence, more prone to bias, confounding and limited ability to establish causality. Studies relying on patient-reported exposures such as self-perceived pre-stroke stress warrant consideration of recall bias when interpreting results. The lower risk of recurrent stroke with anticoagulation in occlusive dissection subgroups is not derived from randomised comparisons, and caution should be exercised when interpreting these data. Beyond study design limitations, there remains limited evidence on which preventive interventions are most effective and feasible in young adults, across different regions and healthcare systems. Results from the ongoing Y-SCOPE study ( NCT06820411 ) assessing optimal prevention strategies and outcome improvement in young ischaemic stroke patients are awaited. Future research should prioritise population-based cohort studies and larger, adequately powered RCTs to provide reliable data for guiding individual patient care and treatment decisions. Outcomes and prognostication Two large meta-analyses demonstrate ongoing high residual recurrence risk in patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA. In a meta-analysis of 171,068 patients with minor stroke or TIA, the pooled incidence of recurrent stroke was 5.94 events per 100 person-years in the first year, with cumulative 5- and 10-year risks of 12.5% and 19.8%, respectively. In another meta-analysis, the cumulative incidence of recurrent ischaemic stroke after AF-related stroke approached 4% per year despite high rates of oral anticoagulation, with even higher rates in patients with stroke despite anticoagulation (7.2% per year). Post-stroke epilepsy (PSE) is associated with increased mortality and reduced quality of life. The ODYSSEY registry showed that the 5-year cumulative risk of PSE after ischaemic stroke and ICH in young adults was 3.7% and 7.6%, respectively, with most presenting seizures occurring in the first year. Cortical involvement and early post-stroke seizure (<7 days) were strongly associated with PSE, and the SELECT and CAVE scores performed well for risk stratification. The PROLEVIS trial compared early administration of levetiracetam with placebo in patients with cortical ischaemic stroke within 14 days; the primary outcome of first symptomatic seizure did not differ between groups (conference presentation; preliminary). In patients with ICH, the Edinburgh Risk Score incorporating APOE genotyping was associated with recurrent ICH during long-term follow-up. In patients with stroke due to carotid atherosclerosis, MRI imaging to detect intra-plaque haemorrhage improved risk stratification when incorporated into a risk score (IMPROVE), identifying patients at greatest risk of recurrent ischaemic stroke receiving best medical therapy. Potential practice implications The long-term risk of recurrent stroke is considerable after minor stroke/TIA and AF-related stroke, highlighting persistent risk beyond the acute

cortical ischaemic stroke within 14 days; the primary outcome of first symptomatic seizure did not differ between groups (conference presentation; preliminary). In patients with ICH, the Edinburgh Risk Score incorporating APOE genotyping was associated with recurrent ICH during long-term follow-up. In patients with stroke due to carotid atherosclerosis, MRI imaging to detect intra-plaque haemorrhage improved risk stratification when incorporated into a risk score (IMPROVE), identifying patients at greatest risk of recurrent ischaemic stroke receiving best medical therapy. Potential practice implications The long-term risk of recurrent stroke is considerable after minor stroke/TIA and AF-related stroke, highlighting persistent risk beyond the acute phase and reinforcing the need to optimise long-term goal-directed secondary prevention. Risk prediction scores might be used to counsel younger patients of their future risk of PSE. Routine administration of prophylactic anti-seizure medication after ischaemic stroke has not demonstrated benefit for seizure prevention. Carotid plaque imaging with high-resolution MRI may improve prognostication of future ischaemic stroke risk and could inform individualised treatment decisions. Key limitations and gaps Future trials of prophylactic anti-seizure medication may inform whether selection of acute ischaemic stroke patients that may benefit from this therapeutic approach can be enriched by identifying high-risk patients using prediction scores. Future RCTs comparing revascularisation with medical therapy may also adopt selection strategies based on risk scores that incorporate MRI markers of plaque vulnerability. More broadly, key remaining gaps include determining which prediction tools and imaging biomarkers should change clinical decisions (including defining actionable thresholds and harmonising how these measures are reported and interpreted across centres) and how to integrate them into clinical pathways. Neurorehabilitation Recent RCTs have evaluated novel neuromodulation and pharmacological approaches for post-stroke rehabilitation with mixed results. The EMAGINE trial, a double-blind, sham-controlled study conducted in the United States, evaluated electromagnetic network targeting field therapy paired with home-based exercise in subacute stroke patients with moderate-to-severe disability. The trial was stopped early after enrolling 100 participants due to futility in the primary endpoint of disability reduction at day 90 (mRS), though a promising trend emerged for functional independence (26% achieved mRS 0–1 in the active group vs 10% in sham group), with no device-related serious adverse events. The TRANSPORT2 phase 2 multicentre triple-blind RCT ( n = 129) found that adding bi-hemispheric transcranial direct current stimulation at 2 or 4 mA to modified constraint-induced movement therapy in patients 1–6 months post-ischaemic stroke did not further reduce upper limb motor impairment compared with modified constraint-induced movement therapy plus sham, though transcranial direct current stimulation was safe, well-tolerated and feasible. ESTREL, a multicentre RCT with 610 participants, reported that adding levodopa/carbidopa to standardised rehabilitation therapy based on active task-oriented training did not significantly improve motor function at 3 months compared with placebo, with no difference in adverse events. A small trial ( n = 43) comparing home-based self-managed rehabilitation programmes (STRONG online platform vs paper exercises) yielded modest motor improvements in both arms, yet STRONG participants reported superior arm/hand use quality and increased self-efficacy, suggesting that accessible home-based delivery can improve functional outcomes. A network meta-analysis of 24 trials including 868 stroke patients suggested that smart rehabilitation therapy combined with transcranial magnetic stimulation had highest effectiveness in improving activities of daily living. The ESO guideline on motor rehabilitation, published in 2025, recommends at least 20 h of additional repetitive upper limb and gait practice, high-intensity walking training in chronic stroke patients with stable cardiovascular status and consideration of behavioural transfer packages for upper limb task-specific training. The SEARCH trial ( n = 158) found that structured visual scanning training for hemianopia showed no superiority over sham training in the primary outcome (visual function questionnaire NEI VFQ-25) from baseline to 26 weeks, yet both groups improved substantially, suggesting robust placebo/expectancy effects warranting further mechanistic research. Potential practice implications Current trial evidence does not support routine use of levodopa to enhance post-stroke motor recovery. In the studied population, bi-hemispheric transcranial direct current stimulation at standard doses was not associated with improved outcomes when added to intensive upper limb rehabilitation. Electromagnetic network targeting field therapy appears safe with promising trends towards improved functional independence; however, larger definitive trials are needed before clinical implementation. Both digital and paper-based home rehabilitation programmes can produce functional gains; online platforms may offer additional benefits for self-efficacy. Providing at least 20 h of additional repetitive upper limb and gait practice is consistent with current ESO motor rehabilitation guideline recommendations, with high-intensity gait training strongly recommended for chronic stroke patients with stable cardiovascular status. Key limitations and gaps Several trials evaluating novel neuromodulation approaches were underpowered or prematurely terminated, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Protocols for optimising dose, combination and delivery of advanced neuromodulation therapies are still being established. Long-term real-world effectiveness and adherence data, particularly for home-based and digital interventions, are needed to guide clinical implementation. Post-stroke cognitive

platforms may offer additional benefits for self-efficacy. Providing at least 20 h of additional repetitive upper limb and gait practice is consistent with current ESO motor rehabilitation guideline recommendations, with high-intensity gait training strongly recommended for chronic stroke patients with stable cardiovascular status. Key limitations and gaps Several trials evaluating novel neuromodulation approaches were underpowered or prematurely terminated, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Protocols for optimising dose, combination and delivery of advanced neuromodulation therapies are still being established. Long-term real-world effectiveness and adherence data, particularly for home-based and digital interventions, are needed to guide clinical implementation. Post-stroke cognitive impairment and dementia Recent evidence in this domain includes identification of risk factors, diagnostic frameworks and therapeutic interventions for post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) and dementia (PSD). The large prospective DEMDAS study investigated risk factors for PSCI and PSD in dementia-free stroke patients followed over 5 years. The cumulative incidence of PSD was 3.1% at 6 months, rising to 8.8% at 5 years. Key risk factors for PSD included greater index stroke severity, older age, lower educational attainment, acute-phase cognitive impairment, lower functional status, AF, metabolic syndrome, stroke recurrence and neuroimaging markers of cerebral small-vessel disease. Metabolic syndrome was strongly associated with late-onset PSD (>6 months), whereas factors related to index stroke severity were more strongly related to early-onset PSD (≤6 months). Patients who received acute reperfusion therapies had a 65% lower risk of PSD. The prospective IDEA3 study demonstrated that stroke patients with positive baseline amyloid PET scans had substantially higher risk of PSD, emphasising the role of co-pathology. Patients with diffusion-weighted imaging-negative TIA exhibited a rate of cognitive decline comparable to that of stroke patients after controlling for vascular risk factors. The newly revised VasCog-2–WSO diagnostic criteria for vascular dementia adopt a spectrum-based framework using the term vascular cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID). Major revisions include requirement that neurocognitive disorder persists for > 3 months, clear temporal relationship between cerebrovascular disease and cognitive decline, integration of fluid and neuroimaging biomarkers, distinction between possible and probable VCID and introduction of a preclinical “at-risk VCID” category. Regarding therapeutic interventions, a meta-analysis of 19 studies ( n = 875) found that computerised cognitive training might enhance general cognitive function in patients with PSCI. Another systematic review reported that brain stimulation therapies, predominantly transcranial direct current stimulation, were associated with improved post-stroke cognitive outcomes. An RCT of cardiorespiratory training starting 2 months post-stroke demonstrated better executive and global cognitive function at 12 months, though it did not influence the primary imaging outcome. A further trial in chronic stroke survivors with executive dysfunction found that strategy training improved immediate societal participation, though the effect did not persist at 3 months. Potential practice implications Diagnostic criteria for vascular dementia were substantially revised. Metabolic syndrome is associated with late-onset PSD, suggesting effective treatment of metabolic syndrome in stroke survivors as a potential prevention target. DWI-negative TIA is associated with cognitive decline after the index event, supporting closer attention to cognitive outcomes and follow-up strategies in this group. Positive amyloid PET status is associated with higher risk of PSCI. Promising novel therapeutic strategies for PSCI include brain stimulation and computerised cognitive training. Cardiorespiratory training after stroke is safe and may improve executive and global cognitive function. Key limitations and gaps Multiple studies investigating PSCI demonstrate high heterogeneity in populations, interventions and outcome measures, necessitating improved standardisation and adequately powered RCTs. Long-term effects of brain stimulation and computerised cognitive training remain unclear. Larger trials are needed to investigate cardiorespiratory training efficacy and define optimal training regimens. Cognitive endpoints should be incorporated into stroke trials given the high prevalence and functional impact of PSCI. The ongoing DISCOVERY trial ( NCT04916210 ) will enrol 8000 dementia-free stroke survivors and aims to elucidate mechanisms of brain resilience and susceptibility to PSCI using clinical, imaging and biomarker data. Systems of care and implementation Recent evidence focused on prehospital delivery models and implementation strategies to shorten time-to-treatment, including mobile stroke units (MSUs) and workflow optimisation for EVT, and adherence to key acute care targets through care bundles. Analysis of the BEST-MSU trial, a multi-site study in 7 US cities, demonstrated that MSU deployment was economically favourable from a Medicare perspective, with lifetime incremental cost-effectiveness ratios of US$94,710 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) overall for IVT-eligible patients and US$31,259/QALY in patients without pre-existing disability. In a separate retrospective observational cohort study using data from 106 US hospitals in the Get With The Guidelines-Stroke registry, prehospital management with MSU was associated with lower global disability at discharge compared with standard emergency medical services in patients potentially eligible for IVT. The Australian MSU-TELEMED programme demonstrated that tele-neurology staffing can be safe, productive and potentially cost-saving, supporting hybrid deployment models (conference presentation; preliminary). The OPTIMAL cluster trial tested a behaviour-change package (PEITER: Persuasion, Enablement, Incentivisation, Training, Education,

cost-effectiveness ratios of US$94,710 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) overall for IVT-eligible patients and US$31,259/QALY in patients without pre-existing disability. In a separate retrospective observational cohort study using data from 106 US hospitals in the Get With The Guidelines-Stroke registry, prehospital management with MSU was associated with lower global disability at discharge compared with standard emergency medical services in patients potentially eligible for IVT. The Australian MSU-TELEMED programme demonstrated that tele-neurology staffing can be safe, productive and potentially cost-saving, supporting hybrid deployment models (conference presentation; preliminary). The OPTIMAL cluster trial tested a behaviour-change package (PEITER: Persuasion, Enablement, Incentivisation, Training, Education, and Review) across 16 hospitals treating 1288 LVO patients with EVT. The intervention was associated with shorter door-to-puncture times and improved 90-day functional outcomes (mRS scores of 0–3) from 55.4% to 66.4% (conference presentation; preliminary). The MAP-STROKE study developed a personalised Bayesian prehospital triage algorithm for suspected LVO patients, with modelling suggesting a 2.1% absolute increase in mRS scores of 0–2 by optimising bypass decisions to comprehensive stroke centres (conference presentation; preliminary). A population-based study of 1821 ICH patients found that achieving early care bundle targets (BP, glucose, oxygen, temperature control) and shorter onset-to-admission times were associated with improved 3-month functional outcomes (mRS scores of 0–3). Potential practice implications Mobile stroke unit deployment may improve functional outcomes and appear cost-effective in high-volume systems, though evidence is primarily from urban settings in the United States and Australia. Workflow behaviour-change packages can reduce treatment delays and were associated with improved outcomes for EVT in a cluster trial setting. Personalised prehospital triage algorithms show promise for optimising LVO patient routing. Early care bundle implementation for ICH was associated with better functional outcomes in a population-based study. Key limitations and gaps Mobile stroke unit evidence is primarily from high-resource and urban settings and cost-effectiveness may differ by geography and service volume. Modelling-based prehospital triage tools (eg, MAP-STROKE) require prospective validation, including assessment of potential harms (eg, overtriage, inappropriate bypass and capacity constraints). The ICH care bundle study was observational, limiting causal inference. Ongoing pre-hospital trials include FASTEST (recombinant factor VIIa in ultra-early ICH) and EAST (prehospital ICH interventions). Other topics Concerning neuroprotection, a post-hoc meta-analysis of individual patient data pooling ESCAPE-NA1, ESCAPE-NEXT and FRONTIER RCTs suggested a potential functional benefit of nerinetide in patients treated within 3 h and selected for reperfusion (56% vs 48% responders at 90 days; adjusted OR 1.48; 95% CI, 1.07–2.06; P = .017), without an apparent safety signal. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in a dedicated phase 3 RCT. Two RCTs evaluated thrombolysis in acute CRAO within 4.5 h. The THEIA trial ( n = 70) compared intravenous alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) with oral aspirin (300 mg) and found no significant difference in visual acuity improvement of at least 0.3 LogMAR at 1 month (66% vs 48%; P = .95). Safety was acceptable, with 1 asymptomatic ICH in the alteplase group and no symptomatic haemorrhages. The TenCRAOS trial ( n = 78) compared intravenous tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg) with aspirin and also showed no benefit for the primary outcome (visual acuity ≤ 0.7 LogMAR at 30 days: 20.0% vs 23.7%, P = .69). However, adverse events occurred more frequently in the tenecteplase group, including one fatal ICH (conference presentation; preliminary). The CLOSURE-AF trial ( n = 912) evaluated left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) vs physician-directed medical care in primary prevention, in patients with AF at high risk of both stroke (mean CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5.2) and bleeding (mean HAS-BLED 3.0). Over a median follow-up of 3 years, LAAO failed to achieve noninferiority for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, cardiovascular or unexplained death or major bleeding (16.83 vs 13.27 per 100 person-years; adjusted HR 1.28, 95% CI, 1.01–1.62) (conference presentation; preliminary). The CREST-2 trial evaluated intensive medical therapy vs carotid revascularisation for asymptomatic high-grade stenosis. In the stenting trial ( n = 1245), carotid artery stenting significantly reduced the 4-year composite endpoint of stroke or death compared with medical therapy alone (2.8% vs 6.0%, P = .02). In the endarterectomy trial ( n = 1240), carotid endarterectomy did not achieve statistical significance (3.7% vs 5.3%, P = .24). These findings suggest that while intensive medical therapy alone yields low stroke rates, the addition of stenting led to a lower risk of a composite of perioperative stroke or death or ipsilateral stroke within 4 years, compared with medical management alone. Carotid endarterectomy did not lead to a significant benefit. Potential practice implications Recent randomised trials (THEIA, TenCRAOS) do not support routine use of intravenous thrombolysis for acute CRAO; enrolment into ongoing RCTs is encouraged. In high-risk AF patients in a primary prevention setting, LAAO failed to demonstrate benefit over best medical therapy in CLOSURE-AF; its role in different risk populations continues to be evaluated in ongoing trials. Carotid artery stenting on top

the addition of stenting led to a lower risk of a composite of perioperative stroke or death or ipsilateral stroke within 4 years, compared with medical management alone. Carotid endarterectomy did not lead to a significant benefit. Potential practice implications Recent randomised trials (THEIA, TenCRAOS) do not support routine use of intravenous thrombolysis for acute CRAO; enrolment into ongoing RCTs is encouraged. In high-risk AF patients in a primary prevention setting, LAAO failed to demonstrate benefit over best medical therapy in CLOSURE-AF; its role in different risk populations continues to be evaluated in ongoing trials. Carotid artery stenting on top of intensive medical management may provide additional benefit in selected patients with asymptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis. Key limitations and gaps Both THEIA and TenCRAOS were likely underpowered and enrolled few patients within 3 h of onset. The larger REVISION trial ( NCT04965038 ), including biomarkers, is ongoing, and results are awaited. Individual patient-level meta-analyses across these trials may further inform whether earlier treatment benefits specific patient subgroups. Following the neutral CLOSURE-AF results, ongoing trials are evaluating left atrial appendage occlusion in different risk populations (CHAMPION-AF, NCT04394546 ; CATALYST, NCT04226547 ; LAAOS-4, NCT05963698 ). For asymptomatic carotid stenosis, the benefit of stenting was based on a small number of events, results from high-volume certified operators may not reflect broader practice, and evolving medical therapies may further reduce the benefit of revascularisation. Discussion This first ESO Annual Stroke Evidence Update summarises major developments in 10 key domains of stroke care in 2025 ( ). Key findings include 3 RCTs showing no benefit of routine EVT over best medical therapy for stroke due to MeVO, refinement of BP targets for ICH with evidence supporting intensive control, validation of polypill strategies for secondary prevention after ICH, and promising data on asundexian, a novel factor XIa inhibitor, for non-cardioembolic stroke ( ). Technological innovations in neuroimaging, particularly photon-counting CT, provide new possibilities for stroke diagnosis and risk assessment, while advances in stroke systems of care, from MSUs and algorithm-based prehospital triage to workflow optimisation and early care bundles, have further demonstrated meaningful improvements in patient outcomes. However, important questions remain. The role of IA thrombolytic therapy following successful EVT and surgical approaches for ICH require further investigation. We have yet to establish the optimal role of rhythm control strategies in secondary stroke prevention, and further research is needed to identify effective therapeutic approaches for AF patients who experience breakthrough stroke. Young stroke populations need better-defined antithrombotic strategies, including long-term, and effective interventions for PSCI are still lacking. Multiple ongoing RCTs are addressing these gaps and will inform future ESO guideline iterations. Regular evidence synthesis has become essential as stroke medicine advances rapidly. This annual update format allows timely dissemination of practice-relevant findings while acknowledging current limitations and identifying research priorities. The ESO Guideline Board remains committed to this initiative as a means of supporting clinicians in delivering evidence-based stroke care and improving patient outcomes worldwide.

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS From 1990 to 2024, the number of registered, enrolment-commenced, published randomised controlled trials increased. Regarding intervention types, rehabilitation, traditional medicine and supportive therapy emerged as the most prevalent. Endovascular therapy or surgery as intervention (compared with traditional medicine) was associated with trial publication. A positive association between target sample size and publication was observed. In addition, the most frequent cause of the termination and withdrawal in trials was the difficulty in enrolment. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Despite notable achievements, numerous hurdles within the design, registration, enrolment and publication remain unresolved and require immediate attention and enhancement, such as the inadequate sample size, retrospective registration, premature termination of enrolment and suppression of study results. Introduction Ischaemic stroke (IS) is always a serious public health problem globally that threatens human life and health. The Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 revealed that stroke ranked as the third leading cause of death and the fourth leading cause of disability-adjusted life years worldwide. Among all new stroke cases, IS accounted for the largest proportion, with 7.8 million cases, representing 65.3%. Characterised by localised blood supply disruption to the brain, IS leads to ischaemia and hypoxia, ultimately causing necrosis and softening of brain tissue. IS often leads to severe and multifaceted outcomes, including physical disabilities such as paralysis and sensory impairments, language disorders, cognitive decline and even death, causing immense suffering for patients and their families and imposing a heavy burden on society. Hence, developing effective and safe treatment strategies is critical. Over the past decades, driven by a pressing need to improve patient outcomes and reduce the burden of this devastating condition, the development of clinical trials for IS has witnessed substantial growth. Researchers and clinicians have initiated numerous randomised controlled trials (RCTs) to investigate and evaluate novel treatment approaches, ranging from pharmacological therapies to sophisticated neuromodulation techniques, therefore furnishing more persuasive evidence for clinical treatment. Moreover, in recent years, investigator-sponsored clinical trials have garnered considerable attention from governments and regulatory authorities in many countries, prompting the implementation of corresponding policies. Until recently, however, there remains a notable lack of research that has thoroughly examined the design, registration, enrolment and publication (DREP) of these RCTs, making it unclear where the research and innovation in the field are going. In addition, the status of the implementation and publication of these trials remains unclear. This may impact the dissemination and application of the study results, as well as the initiation and progression of subsequent trials. Therefore, it is necessary to investigate the development of investigator-sponsored RCTs and outline the treatment landscape of IS. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic analysis using the International Clinical Trial Registry Platform (ICTRP), which features a searchable database containing the trial registration data sets from global providers adhering to criteria for content and quality control. Our aim was to provide a thorough examination of the current global landscape of investigator-sponsored RCTs on IS treatment based on the DREP cycle, pinpoint areas requiring further actions and underscore potential avenues for innovation and enhancement. Methods Study design and data source We conducted a systematic analysis using ICTRP and followed the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) reporting guideline ( ). Searches were conducted from inception to 2 September 2024, with no language restrictions. Specific search strategies were developed ( ). We considered investigator-sponsored RCTs eligible if they enrolled patients with IS for therapeutic purposes. Exclusions comprised those incorporating haemorrhagic stroke, transient ischaemic attack, trials that industries as primary sponsors, single arm trials, non-randomised trials, diagnostic research and duplicate records. In detail, the sponsor of a clinical trial takes responsibility for and initiates the investigation. Duplicate records indicated consistency in the title, registration date, enrolment date, sponsors, inclusion criteria, target size, study design, intervention, outcome, therapeutic time window, contacts and locations, but discrepancies arose solely in the registration number. Duplicate records were first flagged automatically, subsequently undergoing manual verification for accuracy. Trial selection and data extraction Two researchers independently screened potentially eligible trials from search results according to inclusion and exclusion criteria. Likewise, for included trials, data extraction was independently performed by two researchers. Adhere to the DREP cycle, the following information and data were extracted: title, primary sponsor, study design, target sample size, primary purpose, condition, participant gender, participant ages, intervention, allocation, control, primary outcomes, registered number, source registered, registration date, enrolment date, trial status, accessibility of results, etc. Any discrepancies were resolved by consulting the corresponding researcher. The status of clinical trials can be consolidated and categorised into ended, ongoing, temporarily discontinued and unknown status. Trials with status including ‘Completed’, ‘Prematurely ended’, ‘Stopped early’, ‘Terminated’ and ‘Withdrawn’ were considered ended. Status such as ‘Active, not recruiting’, ‘Complete: follow-up complete’, ‘Complete: follow-up

researchers. Adhere to the DREP cycle, the following information and data were extracted: title, primary sponsor, study design, target sample size, primary purpose, condition, participant gender, participant ages, intervention, allocation, control, primary outcomes, registered number, source registered, registration date, enrolment date, trial status, accessibility of results, etc. Any discrepancies were resolved by consulting the corresponding researcher. The status of clinical trials can be consolidated and categorised into ended, ongoing, temporarily discontinued and unknown status. Trials with status including ‘Completed’, ‘Prematurely ended’, ‘Stopped early’, ‘Terminated’ and ‘Withdrawn’ were considered ended. Status such as ‘Active, not recruiting’, ‘Complete: follow-up complete’, ‘Complete: follow-up continuing’, ‘Enrolling by invitation’, ‘Enrolling by invitation’, ‘Not recruiting’, ‘Not yet recruiting’, ‘Ongoing’, ‘Open to recruitment’, ‘Pending recruitment’, ‘Recruiting’ and ‘Recruitment completed’ were deemed ongoing. Trials that hold status like ‘Recruiting stopped after recruiting started’, ‘Suspended’ and ‘Temporary halt’ were classified as temporarily discontinued. If a discrepancy arises between the trial status on primary registration platforms and that listed on the ICTRP, the status recorded on the primary registration platforms shall prevail. Drawing on clinical practice guidelines and the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical coding system for drugs, interventions were primarily classified into the following six categories, encompassing 17 types: endovascular therapy or surgery (encompassing endovascular therapy and surgery), integrated management strategies, medications for central nervous system disorders (encompassing intravenous thrombolysis, antiplatelet medications, anticoagulants, other drugs to improve circulation, neuroprotective agents, medications for risk factor management, anaesthesia and sedation and medications for other central nervous system disorders), rehabilitation and adjuvant therapy (encompassing continuous renal replacement therapy, supportive therapy, nutrition and diet and rehabilitation), therapy for other system disorders and traditional medicine. The definition of traditional medicine was in accordance with WHO standards ( ). Regarding primary outcomes, our particular concern was focused on the top five indicators with the highest frequency: Modified Rankin Scale (mRS), National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), recurrence, death and Barthel Index. Publication status The publication status of the trials encompassed published and unpublished outcomes. Apart from identifying pertinent publications sourced from the primary registration platforms, we conducted a further search in the PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science for trial publications from inception to 4 March 2025 through the clinical trial registry number. Only articles that reported the primary study results in accordance with the registration information were deemed eligible. Reviews, meta-analyses, study protocols, statistical analysis plans and other irrelevant publications without research results were excluded. If more than one publication was obtained for the same registry trial, we selected the earliest article reporting primary outcome results. Data analysis We used descriptive statistics to characterise trial categories. Accordingly, trial characteristics were presented as either the mean with SD for normally distributed continuous variables or the median with IQR for skewed continuous variables, while categorical variables were summarised by the number of subjects with percentages. To compare characteristics between trials, we employed either Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables and χ² or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables, with missing values excluded from the respective analyses. A trend analysis was performed on trial quantities from 1990 to 2024 using the Mann-Kendall trend test, and Sen’s slope estimate was calculated for the annual mean change with the 95% CI. In order to analyse cumulative publication rates since registration and enrolment, the Kaplan-Meier analysis method was applied, with trials censored on 4 March 2025. We conducted a multivariate Cox regression analysis to explore the association of intervention categories, primary outcomes and therapeutic time windows with publication status (also accounting for WHO regions as a covariate), yielding HRs along with their corresponding 95% CI. Based on the distribution of the data, the therapeutic time windows were categorised into four groups, with the demarcation points set at 6 hours, 1 day and 7 days. Examination of Schoenfeld residuals verifies the Cox model’s adherence to proportional hazards assumption ( ). Due to the violation of the proportional hazards assumption regarding the relationship between target sample sizes and publication, we used 3-knot restricted cubic splines (RCS) based on logistic regression analysis to model their relationships, adjusting for intervention categories, primary outcomes, therapeutic time windows and WHO regions, with ORs and 95% CI reported. The internal knots were placed at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of the target sample size distribution to ensure flexible capture of non-linear trends while maintaining stability at the extremes of the data range. Taking into account the influence of trial status and publication timelines, the Cox regression analysis and RCS analysis exclusively encompassed trials that had ended and were registered before 4 March 2020. Additionally, considering a few exceptionally high values on the results, the RCS curve was confined exclusively to the target sample size ranging from 0 to 3000, with the top 13 largest values excluded. We determined the range of target

at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles of the target sample size distribution to ensure flexible capture of non-linear trends while maintaining stability at the extremes of the data range. Taking into account the influence of trial status and publication timelines, the Cox regression analysis and RCS analysis exclusively encompassed trials that had ended and were registered before 4 March 2020. Additionally, considering a few exceptionally high values on the results, the RCS curve was confined exclusively to the target sample size ranging from 0 to 3000, with the top 13 largest values excluded. We determined the range of target sample sizes that exhibited a statistically significant positive association with trial publication using OR and 95% CI from RCS analysis, rounding to nearest integers for practicality. For missing values within therapeutic time windows and target sample sizes in Cox regression analysis and RCS analysis, the median imputation method was used, with sensitivity analyses using multiple imputation techniques. In order to examine the influence of COVID-19 on the annual number of registered, enrolment-commenced and published trials, the Prais-Winsten method was used to conduct interrupted time series analyses, with estimated level change and trend change along with their corresponding 95% CI and adjusted R 2 reported. To ensure balanced representation of pre-COVID-19 and post-COVID-19 periods, we used data spanning from 2016 to 2023. The findings were presented through visual charts and graphs. Lastly, all statistical analyses were conducted using R software V.4.4.2, and a two-sided p value<0.05 indicated statistical significance. Results Search results and basic characteristics Targeted searches returned 5248 records for 4586 trials. Manual review conﬁrmed 1518 records for inclusion, with registration dates from 20 November 2001 to 19 August 2024 and enrolment dates from 21 June 1990 to 1 September 2024. The flow diagram summarised the identification, screening, eligibility and inclusion of the trials ( ). From 1990 to 2024, there was a rising tendency in the number of trials registered (Sen’s slope 4.0 (95% CI 2.8 to 5.1), p<0.001) each year, along with an increase in trials that commenced enrolment (Sen’s slope 3.9 (95% CI 2.9 to 5.0), p<0.001) and were published (Sen’s slope 0.7 (95% CI 0.4 to 1.0), p<0.001) ( ). Regarding countries, China initiated the largest number of RCTs, with a total of 754 (49.7%) trials ( ). A total of 12 countries or regions witnessed an annual average growth rate of trial registration quantities exceeding 10% ( ). In 893 (58.8%) trials, the minimum age for inclusion was set at 18 years. Regarding the maximum age, it was capped at 80 years in 353 (23.3%) trials. Among the included trials, the majority were registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (n=762, 50.2%) and Chinese Clinical Trial Register (n=383, 25.2%). In terms of status, 810 (53.4%) trials were ongoing, and 551 (36.3%) were ended. Among the ended trials, 55 (10.0%) were terminated, and 29 (5.3%) were withdrawn ( ). Intervention strategies and primary outcomes Among the 21 intervention types in all included trials, rehabilitation (n=285, 18.8%), traditional medicine (n=214, 14.1%) and supportive therapy (n=133, 8.8%) emerged as the most prevalent ( ). Regarding the quantity of publication, rehabilitation (n=56, 17.3%), intravenous thrombolysis (n=36, 11.1%) and traditional medicine (n=36, 11.1%) topped the list. In addition, the highest rates of publication were observed for anticoagulants (42.4%) and intravenous thrombolysis (35.6%) ( ). Among medications for risk factor management, antihypertensive medications (n=50, 41.0%) and anticholinergic medications (n=46, 37.7%) contributed the most trials. Regarding therapy for other system disorders, blood and blood products (n=49, 31.0%), and antipsychotic medications (n=23, 14.6%) were the most. In terms of primary outcomes, trials incorporating mRS were the most prevalent, comprising 29.6% (n=450) of the total, followed by those incorporating NIHSS (n=213, 14.0%) ( ). The trials featuring mRS as primary outcome have been published in the highest number, and trials that incorporate death exhibited the highest publication rate ( ). Regarding the cross-distribution of primary outcomes and intervention types, in trials incorporating mRS, notable proportions, specifically 14.0% (n=63) and 12.9% (n=58), featured intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular therapy as the intervention, respectively ( ). Publication rate among all trials The publication search revealed that a total of 323 (21.3%) trials published their study results. Of these trials, the earliest enrolment date was 1 June 1993, and the earliest registration date was 13 July 2004. The cumulative publication rate functions for the time taken to publish since registration and enrolment stratified by years showed steady publication increases annually. Specifically, trials that began enrolment between 2020 and 2024 exhibited faster publication ( ). Of these trials, only 182 (56.3%) were registered prior to enrolment. The median time to publication since registration and enrolment was 4.2 (IQR: 2.8–6.1) years and 4.1 (IQR: 2.5–5.8) years, respectively. Additionally, the median time to enrolment since registration was 55.5 (IQR: 21.0–168.5) days. Moreover, the journals with

enrolment date was 1 June 1993, and the earliest registration date was 13 July 2004. The cumulative publication rate functions for the time taken to publish since registration and enrolment stratified by years showed steady publication increases annually. Specifically, trials that began enrolment between 2020 and 2024 exhibited faster publication ( ). Of these trials, only 182 (56.3%) were registered prior to enrolment. The median time to publication since registration and enrolment was 4.2 (IQR: 2.8–6.1) years and 4.1 (IQR: 2.5–5.8) years, respectively. Additionally, the median time to enrolment since registration was 55.5 (IQR: 21.0–168.5) days. Moreover, the journals with the highest number of publications were Stroke (n=32), The Lancet Neurology (n=15) and Journal of the American Medical Association (n=13). Influencing factors of publication status We identified 435 trials that ended and registered before 4 March 2020, with 189 (43.4%) of them having been published. When comparing published and unpublished trials, there was no statistically significant difference in either the registration date or the enrolment date. For both published and unpublished trials, the majority focused on drug therapy interventions and traditional medicine interventions. Notably, a significant difference in target sample size between published and unpublished trials was shown (p<0.001) ( ). Multivariable Cox regression analysis indicated that endovascular therapy or surgery as intervention (compared with traditional medicine) (HR (95% CI), 2.02 (1.06 to 3.87)) was associated with trial publication ( ). The sensitivity analysis with multiple imputation employed for the missing values within therapeutic time windows revealed similar results ( ). The RCS analysis revealed a positive association between target sample size and publication, when the target sample size exceeds 274, which was supported by an OR of 1.78 (95% CI, 0.99 to 3.19) at a target sample size of 265.2, and an OR of 1.82 (95% CI, 1.01 to 3.28) at a target sample size of 273.3 ( ). In the sensitivity analysis addressing missing values in target sample size through multiple imputation, the statistically significant range for the target sample size was determined to exceed 305 ( ). Obstacles in the implementation of clinical trials Among 551 trials that ended, 29 trials were withdrawn, and 55 were terminated, among which 21 were published. Regarding reasons, a total of 26 (31.0%) trials were terminated or withdrawn due to difficulty in enrolment. Among the terminated trials that were published, the most common reason was the acquisition of positive results ahead of schedule (n=8, 38.1%). As for those trials that were unpublished, apart from enrolment difficulties, the publication of similar trials and the impact of COVID-19 were also contributing reasons. For trials that were withdrawn, the lack of funding also played a role in hindering their initiation to a certain degree ( ). The interrupted time series analyses revealed that the onset of COVID-19 did not exert a notable impact on the number of registered trials, trials initiating enrolment or published trials ( and ). Discussion On conducting an exhaustive search and thorough investigation, our study stands as the most comprehensive analysis of investigator-sponsored RCTs for therapeutic purposes within the realm of IS. We systematically executed a series of progressive endeavours following the DREP cycle: first, unveiling the prevalent landscape and evolving trends in the registration and enrolment; second, charting the progressive trajectory of trials across various intervention types and exploring the intersecting distribution of intervention modalities with primary outcomes of interest; third, elucidating the relationship between potential influencing factors and trial publication; and fourth, investigating the obstacles in the implementation of trials. Based on these progressively advancing endeavours, we presented a comprehensive overview of investigator-sponsored RCTs for therapeutic purposes in IS, synthesised the prevalent challenges and formulated pertinent recommendations for future clinical trials. Our investigation reveals that a considerable number of trials are registered after the enrolment process has already begun, despite the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors’ regulation mandating that clinical trials recruiting participants on or after 1 July 2005 must be registered either at the time of or prior to the enrolment of the first patient as a condition for publication consideration. Furthermore, retrospective registration can give rise to an array of potential risks, including the diminishing trust in research outcomes, the compromise of the scientific method’s credibility and the potential adverse effects on patients and research subjects. Incorporating registration into the ethics approval process stands as a viable solution that enjoys robust backing from researchers. Moreover, it would effectively tackle the deficiency in awareness, which was the most frequently mentioned obstacle to complying with prospective registration. Therefore, in the light of ethical and accountability imperatives, the need to minimise redundant research, promote transparency and reinforce public trust, it is strongly recommended that RCTs be registered on a public trial registry platform before the commencement of enrolment with the initial subject. Moreover, it would effectively tackle the deficiency in awareness, which was the most frequently mentioned obstacle to complying with prospective registration. Therefore, in the light of ethical and accountability imperatives, the need to minimise redundant research, promote transparency and reinforce public trust, it is strongly recommended that RCTs be registered on a public trial registry platform before the commencement of enrolment with the initial subject. In our study, roughly 60% of RCTs have not published their findings, echoing a previous similar study that underscored this issue. This highlights a pressing concern within the treatment of IS, as the non-publication of clinical trial results can result in a lack of transparency and impede the progression of therapeutic interventions. In accordance with the Ottawa statement, it is stipulated that all protocol information and results of clinical trials should be registered and made publicly accessible, which is crucial to uphold research transparency and openness, foster data sharing and collaboration, propel medical research advancements and broaden therapeutic options for patients. Several factors may hinder the publication of these trials, such as research stagnation, non-significant results and the earlier dissemination of similar studies. Given this, it is imperative that we foster the publication and sharing of research results to illuminate the path for the design and execution of future trials in the realm of IS. By consistently accumulating and leveraging evidence and experience, a greater variety of therapeutic strategies can be developed and enhanced, thereby enabling a broader patient population to reap substantial benefits. Future research endeavours are needed to focus intently on exploring specific interventions or outcomes within the realm of IS treatment, while undertaking a more comprehensive and meticulous examination for the publication bias of these trials. Regarding the target sample size, the positive association with publication is potentially due to its capacity to bolster statistical power, mitigate bias and yield more reliable and widely applicable findings, which are generally preferred by journals and peer reviewers, thereby easing the publication process. However, it is important to note that the required sample size varies depending on the research objectives and designs. Another plausible explanation could be that published trials might adopt more scientifically rigorous and logical methodologies for determining sample size, adhere strictly to the research protocol and transparently disclose the sample size calculation methods in their publications, thereby ensuring the reliability of their research outcomes. Hence, it is strongly recommended to engage statisticians during the research design phase for determining an appropriate sample size. Concerning therapeutic time windows, while shorter windows may pose challenges in patient recruitment, our study did not uncover a statistically significant association between therapeutic time windows and trial publication. One conceivable reason could be the heightened interest garnered by trials with shorter therapeutic time windows, which often address acute patient care needs, among both journals and researchers. In clinical practice, therapeutic time windows restrict the use of therapeutic strategies for many patients. While thrombolysis therapy stands as a potent treatment option during the acute phase of IS, its application is circumscribed by a narrow therapeutic window, thereby restricting eligibility for a substantial proportion of patients. Endovascular treatment modalities, such as mechanical thrombectomy, offer a slightly extended window but frequently still suffer from a lack of prompt intervention due to logistical delays, including transfer times and diagnostic procedures. Presently, researchers are engaged in broadening the therapeutic time windows. In addition, the importance of long-term management for IS cannot be overlooked, as it plays a crucial role in facilitating patient recovery and minimising the risk of stroke recurrence. When turning our attention to trials being terminated or withdrawn, the most frequent cause is the challenge of recruitment, which is similar to trials in other fields. Potential reasons may include stringent eligibility criteria, patient apprehension towards unknown risks and inconvenience, geographical constraints, competition among trials and inadequate recruitment strategies and resources. Addressing these issues requires broadening eligibility moderately, enhancing patient education, leveraging technology and fostering collaborations, while continuously monitoring and adapting recruitment efforts to ensure a smooth and seamless enrolment process. Generally, strict selection criteria are essential for enrolling only the most suitable patients in the trial, thereby enhancing internal validity and increasing the likelihood of success. However, these criteria can also pose significant recruitment challenges and limit the generalisability of the study results. By striking a balance between rigorous selection criteria and the practical considerations of recruitment and generalisability, studies that are both valid and informative for the clinical community can be produced. However, these criteria can also pose significant recruitment challenges and limit the generalisability of the study results. By striking a balance between rigorous selection criteria and the practical considerations of recruitment and generalisability, studies that are both valid and informative for the clinical community can be produced. Regarding COVID-19, the interrupted time series analyses did not indicate a notable impact on the quantity of trial registration, enrolment and publication, despite the reported impact of COVID-19 on stroke care. A study revealed that the onset of COVID-19 impacted clinical trial execution at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, leading to fewer hospital visits for blood collection. Consequently, this spurred the adoption of telehealth visits and remote monitoring. In the realm of IS treatment, there has been a growing emphasis on not only established therapeutic approaches such as intravenous thrombolysis, endovascular therapy, antiplatelet medications and risk factor management, but also on the burgeoning fields of rehabilitation and supportive therapy. Furthermore, the therapeutic landscape has expanded to incorporate medications from other system disorders and traditional medicine, reflecting a comprehensive and holistic approach to managing IS. Notably, rehabilitation and traditional medicine constitute a significant proportion of registered RCTs for IS treatment, yet their publication in high-impact journals remains limited. One plausible reason for this could be the inherent ambiguity in some of these interventions, coupled with difficulties in ensuring uniformity in their implementation processes. This leads to variability in study outcomes, hindering meaningful comparisons across research endeavours. Furthermore, studies from the fields of rehabilitation and traditional medicine may struggle to gain favour due to insufficient promotion and advocacy, thereby making it challenging to secure publication in high-impact journals. To facilitate the dissemination of potentially valuable therapeutic strategies to a broader scientific and clinical audience, it is crucial that we accord heightened importance to rehabilitation and traditional medicine treatments, and concurrently strive to improve the rigour and quality of their research design, implementation and report processes. Besides, a multitude of hurdles persists that necessitates attention and resolution. First, despite the growing attention towards rehabilitation and long-term care in recent years, there remains considerable potential for enhancing these treatment modalities and improving patient compliance. Challenges include patient follow-up, condition tracking and prompt adjustment of treatment protocols. Second, the effective management of IS demands seamless integration and cooperation among multiple disciplines, such as neurology, emergency medicine, critical care and others. Nevertheless, interdisciplinary collaboration often faces impediments such as communication barriers, unequal resource allocation and numerous other hurdles, ultimately leading to suboptimal patient outcomes. Last but not least, with the relentless advancement of medical technology and growing patient demands, optimising the allocation of medical resources has emerged as a pressing concern. Addressing this challenge involves rationalising resource allocation, enhancing the accessibility and efficiency of medical services. Essentially, the realm of IS treatment faces a diverse array of challenges. To overcome these obstacles, it is imperative to undertake concerted efforts aimed at enhancing technical expertise, refining patient care strategies, nurturing interdisciplinary cooperation, augmenting research funding and optimising the distribution of medical resources. In our study, some limitations need to be acknowledged and considered. First, the data was sourced from clinical trial registration platforms, where certain data were either outdated or not available in some cases. It is noteworthy, however, that the proportion of such data is insignificant and does not undermine the validity of our findings. Second, despite our utmost endeavours to conduct an exhaustive search of published trials, it was not feasible to include all national/regional databases. Given this, the publication rate of trials might be underestimated to some extent. Third, we did not conduct a comprehensive assessment of publication bias in our study due to the heterogeneity of interventions and outcomes. Despite the challenges, future studies focusing on specific intervention categories or outcome measures should aim to formally assess publication bias where feasible. Fourth, the findings from our regression analysis should be interpreted with caution, as the exclusion of funding source as a covariate may have introduced residual confounding to some extent. Fifth, our study excluded trials involving TIA, considering the homogeneity among the included patient population. Future research is encouraged to investigate the development status and emerging trends of RCTs on TIA treatment. Sixth, our study did not incorporate industry-sponsored clinical trials, considering the heterogeneity of the research purposes and regulations. Future studies are needed to delve deeper into the advancements and challenges of these trials. chunks.content: Introduction This article is an abridged translation of the German guideline, which is available online [ ]. A complete version of this guideline (in German) can be found on the website of the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neurologie ( https://dgn.org/leitlinien ) and the AWMF (Arbeitsgemeinschaft wissenschaftlicher Medizinischer Gesellschaften, https://register.awmf.org/de/leitlinien ). For the current German guideline, key questions were based on the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) questions published by the European Stroke Organization (ESO) guideline in 2017 [ ]. Therefore, only new or updated recommendations are presented in this overview. Definition CVT is defined as a rare form of stroke where thrombosis occurs in the venous side of the brain circulation leading to obstruction of one or more cerebral veins and / or dural venous sinus. Methods of guideline development This guideline is registered with www.awmf.org under 030/098. Level of evidence: S2k. Date of last update: 24.10.2023. Valid until: 23.10.2023. Edited by: Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neurologie e. V. (DGN). Joint recommendations / Societies participating in guideline development: Deutsche Schlaganfall-Gesellschaft e.V. (DSG) Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neuroradiologie e.V. (DGNR) Deutsche Gesellschaft für Kinder- und Jugendmedizin e.V. (DGKJ) Deutsche Gesellschaft für Angiologie-Gesellschaft für Gefäßmedizin e.V. (DGA) Gesellschaft für Thrombose und Hämostaseforschung e. V. (GTH) Gesellschaft für Pädiatrische Radiologie e. V. (GPR) Österreichische Gesellschaft für Neurologie (ÖGN) Österreichische Schlaganfall-Gesellschaft (ÖGSF) Schweizerische Neurologische Gesellschaft (SNG) We aimed to update the ESO guideline published in 2017 using its existing GRADE questions. To this end, a selective literature review was perfomed to cover the time since last systematic review performed by the ESO guideline panel. All topics were worked on by author-teams and then coordinated in a first Delphi round by the guideline group. A strong recommendation corresponds in the formulation to a “shall”, a moderate recommendation to a “should” and an open recommendation to a “can”. In a second Delphi round, all recommendations were finally agreed upon by the guidelines group. Based on this expert consensus, the formulation of the core statements was evaluated as strong agreement in the case of > 95% of all experts, as moderate agreement in the case of > 75–95%, as majority agreement in the case of > 50–75%, and as no agreement in the case of ≤ 50%. In this abbreviated guideline we only refer to agreements of 90–100%. The guideline was reviewed by the Guideline Committee of the German Neurological Society (DGN) and approved by the DGN. Interdisciplinarity was established. Patient organizations were not involved. All participants in the guideline have submitted their declarations of interest (AWMF form for the declaration of interests in the context of guideline projects) to the coordinator and the Editorial Office for Guidelines of the DGN in time and completely filled out. The evaluation of the declarations of interest with regard to thematic relevance to the guideline was carried out by CW and the Editorial Office for Guidelines of the DGN. An external evaluation of the declarations of interest of CW was carried out by an independent reviewer of the DGN. Less than 50% of authors reported potential conflicts of interest for direct oral anticoagulants and abstined from the vote on the respective recommendation. For reasons of transparency, the interests of the participants and the consequences drawn therefrom are listed on the respective AWMF guideline website. This guideline has been produced without any influence or support from industry and is provided by the authors free of charge. Preliminary note In patients with septic CVT, the initial focus is on eliminating the focus of infection and on antibiotic treatment, which is not part of this guideline. Otherwise, treatment does not differ from aseptic CVT, and therefore septic CVT is not discussed separately. Diagnosis If CVT is clinically suspected, cerebral imaging is the most important diagnostic test. Digital subtraction angiography is only rarely indicated if the other imaging procedures do not provide congruent findings. Otherwise, it plays practically no role in the diagnosis of CVT today. Key question: In patients suspected of CVT, should computed tomography with venous angiography versus magnetic resonance imaging with venous angiography be used to diagnose CVT? Key question: In patients suspected of acute CVT should D-dimer be measured before neuroimaging to diagnose CVT? Key question: In patients with CVT, does a policy of screening for thrombophilia prevent recurrent venous thrombosis, reduce death and improve functional outcome? Even if there is a lack of study data proving a benefit of etiologic workup, it is still useful to identify the relevant risk factors suspected to have contributed to the thrombosis in every patient with CVT, as this can have an influence on treatment and secondary prophylaxis. The most common risk factors or causes of CVT include [ ]: Female gender (75%) Combined hormonal contraceptives (40–50% of all women with CVT) Thrombophilia (34–40%) Pregnancy (especially in the 3rd trimester) and postpartum phase

does a policy of screening for thrombophilia prevent recurrent venous thrombosis, reduce death and improve functional outcome? Even if there is a lack of study data proving a benefit of etiologic workup, it is still useful to identify the relevant risk factors suspected to have contributed to the thrombosis in every patient with CVT, as this can have an influence on treatment and secondary prophylaxis. The most common risk factors or causes of CVT include [ ]: Female gender (75%) Combined hormonal contraceptives (40–50% of all women with CVT) Thrombophilia (34–40%) Pregnancy (especially in the 3rd trimester) and postpartum phase (10–20%) Local infections, e.g. otitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis, stomatitis, dental abscesses, meningitis, brain abscess (≈10%) JAK2V617F mutation (6–7%) Myeloproliferative disease (4%) Hormone replacement therapy (3–4%) Cerebral neoplasia (≈2%) Idiopathic (10–20%) Other rare risk factors or comorbidities: Disseminated intravascular coagulation Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Vaccine-induced prothrombotic immunogenic thrombocytopenia (VITT) Severe hyperhomocysteinemia Dysfibrinogenemia Malignancies: carcinomas, lymphomas, carcinoid, leukemias Sickle cell anemia, hypochromic or hemolytic anemia Collagenoses: lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's syndrome Vasculitides: Behçet's disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA; formerly: Wegener's granulomatosis) Sarcoidosis Very rare causes are Intracranial hypotension (cerebrospinal fluid hypotension syndrome) Lumbar cerebrospinal fluid puncture: CVT can occur with a time delay after a cerebrospinal fluid puncture. In these cases, in contrast to CSF hypotension syndrome, the headache usually increases when lying down. Local: craniocerebral trauma, neurosurgical operations, mechanical outflow obstruction due to tumors Disorders with venous stasis: central venous catheters, strangulation, dural arteriovenous malformation Drug-related toxic causes: Androgens, chemotherapeutic agents, corticosteroids, erythropoietin, vitamin A overdose, E. coli-derived asparaginase in combination with prednisone, illegal drugs Metabolic diseases: Diabetes mellitus, thyrotoxicosis, uremia, nephrotic syndrome Gastrointestinal tract diseases: liver cirrhosis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis Cardiac diseases: heart failure, cardiomyopathy Generalized infectious diseases: Bacterial: septicemia, endocarditis, typhoid fever, tuberculosis Viral: measles, hepatitis, encephalitis (HSV, HIV), cytomegalovirus Parasitic: malaria, trichinosis Fungal infections: Aspergillosis For children with CVT, the causes listed in the literature are [ ]: Thrombophilia Dehydration Perinatal complications Infections Solid tumors Hemato-oncological diseases In children and adolescents with venous thrombosis, including CVT, the correlation between the initial manifestation of thrombosis or thromboembolic recurrences and congenital thrombophilic risk factors is more pronounced than in adults [ , ]. Therapy Anticoagulation in the acute phase of CVT is essential to prevent propagation of the thrombus or renewed thrombotic occlusion of vessel sections that have already been reopened by the body's own fibrinolysis. Anticoagulation is also indicated in case of intracranial bleeding due to venous congestion from CVT. There are 3 treatment phases in anticoagulant therapy like for venous thrombosis (Fig. ) [ ]. Treatment is usually initiated with parenteral anticoagulation (initial phase) before switching to a maintenance regimen, usually with an oral anticoagulant. At the end of maintenance phase, anticoagulation is either discontinued or, only in case of an increased risk of recurrence, continued as secondary prophylaxis. Anticoagulation in the acute phase During the acute phase, treatment should take place under monitoring conditions in a stroke unit (or intensive care unit if necessary) in order to recognize and treat any clinical deterioration or complications at an early stage. A transfer to a center with interventional neuroradiology and neurosurgery is recommended at the latest when signs of intracranial pressure appear. Due to individual courses with more or less pronounced neurological symptoms and varying risks of bleeding and recurrence, the acute phase is not defined in terms of time. Therefore, stable or oligosymptomatic (e.g. isolated headache) patients without evidence of bleeding can be treated like in maintenance therapy, on a normal ward or primarily on an outpatient basis. Key question: In patients with acute CVT, does anticoagulation improve clinical outcome compared to no anticoagulation? Key question: In patients with acute CVT does low molecular weight heparine (LMWH) improve clinical outcome compared to unfractionated heparine (UFH)? As treatment with LMWH does not require intravenous access or regular laboratory checks, it is also preferable in practical use, as it has been shown to be more effective and safer than UFH in individual studies and meta-analyses [ , ]. Advantages are the easier application through once or twice daily subcutaneous injections [ ], the lack of need for laboratory monitoring and frequent dose adjustments as well as a lower risk of developing heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) type II. The European guideline on the treatment of CVT therefore recommends treatment with weight-adapted LMWH, as does the AWMF S2k guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism [ , ]. There is a significant restriction on the use of LMWH in patients with advanced renal insufficiency. However, the overall evidence regarding the comparison of LMWH and UFH in patients with CVT is low. The randomized trial and prospective observational study presented were associated with a high risk of bias and a systematic literature review with meta-analysis of three studies

of developing heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) type II. The European guideline on the treatment of CVT therefore recommends treatment with weight-adapted LMWH, as does the AWMF S2k guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism [ , ]. There is a significant restriction on the use of LMWH in patients with advanced renal insufficiency. However, the overall evidence regarding the comparison of LMWH and UFH in patients with CVT is low. The randomized trial and prospective observational study presented were associated with a high risk of bias and a systematic literature review with meta-analysis of three studies (179 patients under LMWH, 352 patients under UFH) failed to demonstrate a significant difference in mortality or functional outcome [ ]. UFH has a possible advantage in patients requiring intensive care who may require short-term surgical intervention, as coagulation normalizes within one to two hours after the end of intravenous heparin therapy. Patients who have a contraindication to the use of LMWH (severe renal insufficiency) should also be treated with UFH. There are currently no randomized studies on the use of direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) in the acute phase of CVT. In contrast to the treatment of VTE, no recommendation can therefore currently be made on their use in the acute phase of CVT. Instead, clinical stabilization under heparin treatment should be awaited first. Thrombectomy und Thrombolysis Neuroradiological interventional therapy is based on transvenous mechanical thrombectomy using stent retrievers and/or aspiration catheters. Transarterial lysis therapy is no longer performed. At the discretion of the neurointerventionalist, local (catheter-directed) thrombolysis may be used as an adjunct to mechanical thrombectomy in individual cases. Key question: Does endovascular recanalization improve clinical outcome compared to anticoagulation in patients with acute cerebral venous thrombosis? A randomized trial (TO-ACT) in patients at high risk of poor clinical outcome (defined as at least one of the following risk factors: qualitative or quantitative impairment of consciousness, parenchymal hemorrhage or deep cerebral vein thrombosis) was terminated prematurely and showed no benefit of endovascular thrombolysis with or without thrombectomy versus therapeutic anticoagulation [ ]. The other data published to date are based on retrospective and uncontrolled case series and mostly examined local thrombolysis with alteplase or urokinase, in some cases with thrombectomy by aspiration, stent retriever thrombectomy, or balloon-guided thrombectomy/angioplasty with stent placement [ ]. A meta-analysis was unable to demonstrate any difference between the procedures used [ ]. Thus, although local thrombolysis alone or in combination with thrombectomy has high recanalization rates, it is associated with higher overall bleeding complications, with no evidence of improved clinical outcome to date. Patients with CVT who have a low risk of poor clinical outcome are therefore unlikely to be suitable candidates for local thrombolysis. In patients with large space-occupying hemorrhagic infarcts, thrombolytic therapy can lead to an increase in the size of the hemorrhage and thus accelerate the process of impending entrapment. In individual cases, endovascular recanalization, either as venous thrombectomy alone or in combination with thrombolysis, can be considered as an individual treatment attempt in a specialized (neurointerventional) center for other patients who deteriorate under adequate anticoagulation. Intracranial pressure therapy Although cerebral edema can be detected on imaging in up to 50% of all patients with CVT, specific measures to reduce intracranial pressure are only necessary in a small number of cases. Key question: For patients with acute CVT and parenchymal lesion(s) with impending herniation, does decompressive surgery (hemicraniectomy or haematoma evacuation) improve outcome, compared with conservative treatment? There are no current or anticipated randomized studies on this question, but several partly controlled case series and current reviews [ , ]. Even if the overall number of cases is small, the results consistently indicate that deaths can be prevented by means of surgical decompression in the event of imminent incarceration without simultaneously leading to an increase in the proportion of severely disabled patients. In addition, some cases are reported in which a good functional result was achieved despite advanced clinical signs of herniation. Anticoagulation in the maintenance phase The duration of the acute phase of CVT varies, and the associated decision for anticoagulation must be made on an individual basis and depending on the patient's symptoms and complications. Maintenance therapy therefore begins after clinical stabilization and usually after monitoring phase. At this point, the aim in everyday clinical practice is to switch from parenteral to oral anticoagulation. DOAC and vitamin K antagonists (VKA) are available for this purpose. Key question: In patients with cerebral venous thrombosis, does treatment with DOAC improve clinical outcome, reduce major haemorrhagic complications and reduce thrombotic recurrences, compared to conventional anticoagulation (heparin and VKA)? In large studies in patients with atrial fibrillation or lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, DOAC have shown a significantly better safety profile compared to VKA with comparable efficacy. In addition to numerous
